flagged.script: The check is a GROUP BY. Put the test advertisers into buckets by score, and in each bucket compare two numbers: the average score, and the share who really churned. Take the bucket scored between 20 and 30 percent. The model said about 25 percent on average, and about 33 percent left. One in four promised, one in three delivered. The next bucket up, the thirties, was promised about 35 percent and delivered about 40. When predicted and actual agree in every bucket, a model is called calibrated: its 30 percent means 30 in a hundred. This one runs low on both sides of 30.

flagged.script: Now every bucket at once. For a calibrated model, each bucket's prediction and its actual rate would match. Here the actual rate is above the prediction in all eight buckets, from the safest advertisers to the riskiest. flagged.script: Start with one advertiser. Say the model predicted 3,000 dollars and they spent 2,000. The miss is 1,000 dollars. Do that for every test advertiser, ignore whether each miss was high or low, and average. That is the mean absolute error, MAE: the average miss, in dollars. As always, it needs a bar to beat. The laziest forecast says each advertiser will spend what they spent in the last eight weeks. It misses by about 2,400 dollars. A sharper one doubles the most recent four weeks. Call it the run-rate. It misses by about 2,000 dollars, and that is the bar.

flagged.script: Both candidates clear the bar. Model A misses by about 1,730 dollars on average. Model B misses by about 1,680. So B wins, by 58 dollars. Before you believe that, ask how much of the 58 is luck. Score the same two models on a different draw of advertisers and the gap moves. Here it could plausibly sit anywhere from 177 dollars in B's favour to 73 in A's. That range crosses zero. On average miss, then, this is a tie. More on that check in the next lesson.

flagged.script: Now a second way to keep score. Picture two made-up models and 100 advertisers. The first is off by 1,000 dollars on every single one. The second is exactly right on 99 of them and off by 100,000 dollars on the last. Same MAE: 1,000 dollars each. Would finance call them equally good? The second measure says no. Square every miss, average the squares, then take the square root to get back to dollars. That is root mean squared error, RMSE. Squaring means a miss ten times bigger counts a hundred times more. The steady model scores 1,000. The model with one disaster scores 10,000.

flagged.script: Models are no different. A model's score is measured on a sample too. The churn model's AUC of about 0.85 comes from 4,000 test advertisers. Draw a different set and it could land anywhere from about 0.83 to 0.86. So when the assistant says a new model is better by a hair, ask for an interval on the gap between the two, measured on the same test rows. Last lesson's 58 dollar gap between model A and model B is the example. Its interval runs from 177 dollars one way to 73 the other. Zero is inside. Call it a tie, and keep the simpler model.

flagged.script: The fix is a change of scale, not a cleverer model. Put spend on a log scale, the kind you pick for a chart axis when one bar dwarfs the rest. There, one thousand dollars to ten thousand is the same step as ten thousand to a hundred thousand. Equal steps are equal percentage changes, so the giants no longer dominate. Fit the same weighted sum to the log of spend, and the average miss falls to about 1,430 dollars, the best so far. It even edges out a more flexible kind of model fitted in dollars, which gets to about 1,500. The interval on that gap only just clears zero.

flagged.script: The assistant hands back eighty lines of Python and one proud sentence: AUC 0.98. You could not have written those eighty lines. You do not need to. Every modelling script, whoever wrote it, has the same six parts in the same order. If you can find them, you can audit the script, because each of the classic bugs lives in one particular part and shows up as one recognisable line. By the end of this lesson you will know which line produced that 0.98, and what the honest number was.

flagged.script: Monday morning the risk list goes out. By ten, an account manager is at your desk about one name on it. The advertiser's ID ends in 754, and the list says 73 percent. Her question is fair: why? Because the model said so is not something she can take into a call. There are three questions you can put to any model. What does it lean on overall? How does its answer move when one column changes? And why this advertiser? Each has a standard tool, and each tool has a limit that belongs in the same breath as the answer.

flagged.script: The usual reply is: then control for it. Ask the assistant to compare like with like, holding tenure, spend, vertical and the rest fixed. That is what a regression weight does. The naive gap was about 11 points. Adjusted, it shrinks to about six and a half. The truth is still about 2. Adjusting removed the part of the mirage the table can see. It cannot remove the part that comes from a trait nobody recorded. And nothing in the output warns you how far off it still is. Adjusted is a better description. It is still not the effect of acting.

flagged.script: Before you quote 2.8 percent, look at where it came from. This series has a version with seven planted incidents, kept for a later lesson. These scores use the version without them, so forecast error is not mixed up with outage days. And this world is stable by construction, with a model of the same form as the equation that generated it. It was even handed the holiday dates. That is a best case, and a real series, with breaks nobody planned, will score worse. What carries over is the order of work, not the number. Now try it: one forecast, made on the first of March. Switch between the methods and see where each parts from what happened.

flagged.script: The honest test is called backtesting, and it is a rehearsal. Pick a past date and pretend it is today. Train on nothing after it. Forecast the next 28 days. Score that against what happened. Then move on a month and repeat. Last lesson's scores came from twelve of these, because one rehearsal can be lucky. The trend model's monthly miss ranged from about 2 percent to about 3 and a half. One month alone shows nothing of that spread.

flagged.script: A harder test for the trend model and the four week average. From the first of November everything steps up by 12 percent and stays there, and neither is told. In November both are badly wrong. The four week average has a short memory: by December its error is exactly what it would have been. The trend model fits its whole history, so it keeps blending the new level with the old: still about 8 percent off in December and January. March looks normal, then April is off again. Quick to recover is not the same as accurate, though. The four week average's ordinary error from December to April runs from 3 to 10 percent. Even damaged, the trend model was closer in three of those five months.

It sits under 2 and a half percent away from the forecast. A 12 percent drop hides inside the first and only just clears the second. Two of its five days were flagged, and a slightly wider band would have missed it. The sharper the expectation, the smaller the problem you can see. Now the caveat. This forecast has the same form as the equation that generated the series, in a world that never changes. No false alarms is a best case. On a real series, expect more.
